subject: Government
title: Colonial and Constitutional Developments
outline: British colonial administration and the amalgamation of 1914
Indirect Rule: meaning, operation, merits and demerits
British Indirect Rule compared with French assimilation and association
Nigerian constitutions from Clifford (1922) to Independence (1960)
Republican, military and post-military constitutions up to 1999

modules.title: Module 1: Colonial Administration and Indirect Rule
modules.html:
British presence in Nigeria grew from the annexation of Lagos in 1861, through the Oil Rivers/Niger Coast Protectorate and the Royal Niger Company charter, to the proclamation of the Protectorates of Northern and Southern Nigeria in 1900. In 1914 Sir Frederick Lugard amalgamated the Northern and Southern Protectorates with the Colony of Lagos to form the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria.

Reasons for the 1914 Amalgamation

  1. To use the surplus revenue of the South to finance the deficit of the North
  2. Administrative convenience and uniformity of policy
  3. Unification of the railway, currency and judicial systems
  4. Economy of personnel and reduction of administrative cost

Indirect Rule

Indirect Rule is a system of administration in which the colonial power governs the people through their traditional rulers and institutions, under the supervision of British officials.

Structure: Governor → Lieutenant-Governor → Resident (province) → District Officer → Native Authority (Emir/Oba/Warrant Chief) with Native Courts and a Native Treasury (Beit-el-Mal).

Reasons for Its Adoption

  • Shortage of British personnel and funds
  • Vastness of the territory and poor communication
  • Existence of ready-made traditional institutions, especially in the North
  • Language barrier and the desire to avoid resistance
  • Belief that gradual, evolutionary change was best

Merits and Demerits

MeritsDemerits
Cheap to operate; few British officers requiredMade chiefs autocratic and accountable to the British, not the people
Preserved traditional institutions and cultureFailed in the East where there were no chiefs; produced Warrant Chiefs and the 1929 riot
Trained locals in administration and taxationRetarded the political education of the elite and excluded the educated class
Reduced friction and resistanceDeepened North-South divergence and hindered national unity

examples.q: Explain the statement that the 1914 amalgamation was 'a marriage of convenience'.
examples.a: The amalgamation was driven by British administrative and financial interest rather than the wishes of Nigerians. The prosperous South subsidised the deficit-ridden North, and one administration was cheaper to run. The two protectorates continued to be governed separately in practice, with different systems of local administration, education and law, so unity was formal rather than real. This left behind structural divisions that later fuelled regionalism.

examples.q: Compare Indirect Rule in Northern Nigeria with its operation in the East.
examples.a: In the North, Lugard superimposed Residents on an existing centralised hierarchy of Emirs, district and village heads, backed by Sharia courts and an established tax system, so it worked smoothly and cheaply. In the East, there were no centralised rulers, so the British created Warrant Chiefs who lacked legitimacy and abused their authority; taxation was resented, and popular resistance culminated in the Aba Women's Riot of 1929, forcing reform of the system.

modules.title: Module 2: British and French Colonial Policies Compared
modules.html:
France governed her West African territories through the policies of assimilation and later association.

Assimilation

The aim was to convert Africans into black Frenchmen by imposing French language, culture, law and institutions. The four communes of Senegal (Dakar, Goree, Rufisque and Saint-Louis) elected a deputy to the French Parliament, and their inhabitants were French citizens. Elsewhere, Africans were sujets (subjects) governed under the harsh indigenat code, subject to forced labour (corvee). A subject could become an evolue (assimilated citizen) by satisfying strict conditions of literacy in French, monogamy, Christianity, military service and good conduct.

Association

After assimilation proved impracticable and costly, France adopted association: a partnership in which African institutions were partially tolerated while France retained firm central control from Paris through the Governor-General at Dakar.

Comparison of British and French Systems

BasisBritish Indirect RuleFrench Assimilation
AimPreserve local institutionsConvert Africans into Frenchmen
AdministrationDecentralised through chiefsHighly centralised from Paris/Dakar
Role of chiefsRetained with real authorityWeakened; chiefs were mere agents
CultureRespected local cultureSuppressed local culture
Status of citizensBritish subjects/protected personsCitizens (communes) and subjects
LegacyFederalism, regionalismUnitary systems, strong French ties

examples.q: Why did the French abandon the policy of assimilation for association?
examples.a: Assimilation was expensive, since it required extending French education, citizenship rights and institutions to millions of Africans. It was also resisted by Africans who did not wish to abandon their culture, and opposed by French settlers and administrators who feared African representation in Paris. Cultural differences made wholesale conversion impracticable, so France adopted association, which retained central control while tolerating some indigenous institutions.

examples.q: State two similarities between British and French colonial rule in West Africa.
examples.a: Both were imperial systems designed to serve the economic interests of the metropolitan power through the export of raw materials and the import of manufactured goods. Both also relied on African intermediaries and African-funded administration through taxation, and both denied the colonised full political self-determination until nationalist pressure forced constitutional concessions.

modules.title: Module 3: Nigerian Constitutions, 1922 to 1960
modules.html:
Clifford Constitution (1922)

Introduced by Sir Hugh Clifford. Features: created a Legislative Council of 46 members for the Colony and Southern Provinces; introduced the elective principle for the first time in British West Africa — three elected members for Lagos and one for Calabar, on a restrictive franchise requiring 12 months' residence and a gross income of £100 per annum. The North was governed by proclamation. Merit: it stimulated the formation of the first political party, the NNDP (Herbert Macaulay, 1923), and a nationalist press. Demerit: limited franchise, no African majority, no legislative role for the North.

Richards Constitution (1946)

Introduced by Sir Arthur Richards. Features: for the first time brought the North and South under one Legislative Council; created three regions (Northern, Western, Eastern) with Regional Houses of Assembly (and a House of Chiefs in the North); increased unofficial African majority. Demerits: no elections beyond Lagos and Calabar; Nigerians were not consulted before its imposition; regional houses were merely advisory. It is credited with laying the foundation of Nigerian federalism.

Macpherson Constitution (1951)

Preceded by wide consultation from village to national level. Features: a central Council of Ministers with African members; a 148-member House of Representatives; regional legislatures with law-making powers; a quasi-federal structure. Demerits: ministers had no portfolios and no collective responsibility; conflict between the centre and regions produced the 1953 self-government motion crisis and the Kano riot, leading to its collapse.

Lyttleton Constitution (1954)

Established a genuine federal system. Features: Nigeria formally became a federation of three regions plus the Federal Territory of Lagos; exclusive, concurrent and residual legislative lists; regional premiers and regional public/judicial services; regionalisation of the judiciary and marketing boards; the Governor-General presided at the centre. It allowed regions to become self-governing at their own pace: the West and East in 1957, the North in 1959.

Independence Constitution (1960)

Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960 as a federation within the Commonwealth. Queen Elizabeth II remained Head of State, represented by Governor-General Nnamdi Azikiwe; Abubakar Tafawa Balewa was Prime Minister. The Privy Council in London remained the final court of appeal, and a bill of rights was entrenched.

Republican Constitution (1963)

Nigeria became a Federal Republic on 1 October 1963: the Queen ceased to be Head of State; Nnamdi Azikiwe became the first ceremonial President; the Supreme Court of Nigeria replaced the Privy Council as the final appellate court; the Mid-Western Region had been created in 1963, making four regions.

Later Constitutions

  • 1979 — introduced the American-style presidential system, an executive President, federal character principle, and 19 states.
  • 1989 — Babangida's transition constitution, providing for a two-party system (SDP and NRC); never fully operative.
  • 1993 and 1995 — aborted transition documents.
  • 1999 — the current constitution, restoring civil rule on 29 May 1999 with an executive President, bicameral National Assembly, 36 states and 774 local governments.

examples.q: Why is the Richards Constitution of 1946 regarded as the foundation of Nigerian federalism despite its shortcomings?
examples.a: It created three regions, each with its own House of Assembly, and for the first time brought the North and South under a single Legislative Council. Although the regional houses were only advisory and there were no new elections, the regional framework it established became the structural basis on which the Macpherson (1951) and Lyttleton (1954) constitutions built a full federation.

examples.q: Identify two major defects of the Macpherson Constitution that led to its collapse.
examples.a: First, ministers were appointed without portfolios and without collective responsibility, so the Council of Ministers could not function as a cabinet. Second, the relationship between the centre and the regions was ambiguous, and regional legislatures could frustrate central policy. These weaknesses were exposed during the 1953 self-government motion crisis and the Kano riot, forcing the Lyttleton constitutional conference.

quiz.q: The amalgamation of Northern and Southern Nigeria took place in
quiz.solution: Lugard amalgamated the two protectorates with the Colony of Lagos in 1914.

quiz.q: The elective principle was first introduced into Nigeria by the
quiz.solution: The Clifford Constitution of 1922 provided for four elected seats — three in Lagos and one in Calabar.

quiz.q: Under the Clifford Constitution, a voter had to earn an annual gross income of at least
quiz.solution: The franchise was restricted to adult males with 12 months' residence and £100 gross annual income.

quiz.q: The first political party in Nigeria, the NNDP, was formed in 1923 by
quiz.solution: Herbert Macaulay founded the Nigerian National Democratic Party in response to the Clifford Constitution.

quiz.q: Which constitution first brought the North and the South under one legislative council?
quiz.solution: The Richards Constitution united the North and South in a single Legislative Council.

quiz.q: The constitution that established a true federal system in Nigeria was the
quiz.solution: The Lyttleton Constitution of 1954 created a genuine federation with clearly divided legislative lists.

quiz.q: Under the Independence Constitution of 1960, the Head of State was
quiz.solution: Nigeria remained a constitutional monarchy in 1960 with the Queen as Head of State, represented by the Governor-General.
The Republican Constitution took effect on 1 October 1963 with Azikiwe as ceremonial President.

quiz.q: Under Indirect Rule, the British officer in charge of a province was the
quiz.solution: Residents supervised provinces, while District Officers handled districts.

quiz.q: The French policy that sought to turn Africans into black Frenchmen was
quiz.solution: Assimilation aimed at cultural and political absorption into France.

quiz.q: The four communes of Senegal enjoyed
options: Full French citizenship and representation in Paris
quiz.solution: Inhabitants of Dakar, Goree, Rufisque and Saint-Louis were French citizens who elected a deputy to the French Parliament.

quiz.q: The harsh code applied to French African subjects was known as
quiz.solution: The indigenat allowed summary punishment of subjects without trial.

quiz.q: The Western and Eastern Regions became self-governing in
quiz.solution: Both regions attained internal self-government in 1957; the North followed in 1959.

quiz.q: Which constitution introduced the presidential system into Nigeria?
quiz.solution: The 1979 Constitution replaced the parliamentary system with an American-style executive presidency.

quiz.q: A major criticism of Indirect Rule is that it
options: Excluded the educated elite from governance
quiz.solution: Indirect Rule empowered chiefs while sidelining the Western-educated nationalists, delaying political development.

quiz.q: The Privy Council in London ceased to be Nigeria's final court of appeal under the
quiz.solution: The 1963 Republican Constitution made the Supreme Court of Nigeria the final appellate court.
